section.title: Max and Moritz set up a communication channel on &chat_client;
section.para: Hushphone users Max and Moritz demonstrate how groups and contacts are set up using the &program_name; voucher system.

step.para: Max opens the Hushphone app. Hushphone prompts him to enter a name. This name is arbitrary, but it cannot be changed later. Max enters his name and taps Continue.
Max proceeds to the group options by tapping Create or join a group.
Max chooses the Start a new group workflow by tapping that option.
Max names his group West Group. This is the name that Max will see, not what anybody else will see. Max can change the name at any time. After entering the name, he taps Create.

Max is done creating the group. Its name is displayed at the top of the screen, where we see that there are no other members yet. Potential new members need to create vouchers and submit them to Max out-of-band, as shown in the next procedure involving Moritz.

section.title: Moritz prepares to join a group and create a voucher

step.para: Like Max, the first thing Moritz does is provide an arbitrary but permanent name.
Next, Moritz begins group configuration.
Unlike Max, who chose the Start a new group workflow,Moritz chooses the Join someone's group workflow by tapping that option.

Even though Moritz plans on joining an existing group (as you probably guessed, that group is Max's West Group), he must create his own local group. All groups are really local, and owned by their creater, but with a voucher, you can obtain permissions to see what's happening in other people's groups, and your local group is a window into that.
Moritz names his group East Group and taps Get a voucher.
The &program_name; mixnet takes a while to set up Moritz's group and to issue a voucher.
When the voucher (which contains an ID and a read permission for East Group) is ready, Hushphone offers several ways to pass it to Max – as a QR code, as a string of text, or encoded onto a sound.

section.para: The next procedure shows how the voucher gets from Moritz to Max and how Max inducts his new group member.

section.para: This section describes how to configure and use &chat_client; for secure, anonymous communication.
Like many other chat clients, &chat_client; exhibits two panes, one for contacts and one for messages, and a number of communication modes such as text chat, file transfer, and voice.
The following screen capture shows &chat_client; as it appears when opened for the first time.

caption.para: Figure 1. This screen capture shows the elements of the &chat_client; client interface prior to configuration or use.

section.para:
&chat_client; consists of a menu bar, a toolbar, two panes, and a status bar (not visible).
The Conversations and contacts pane displays existing conversations and the contacts specific to them.
The Messages pane displays the title of the selected conversation (if any), its message log, an Invite a contact button for adding new participants, and a text box near the bottom for typing new messages.
Buttons in the toolbar include New conversation (opening a dialog to configure a conversation), Accept invitation (opening a dialog to accept or refuse an invitation from another user), Documentation (activating, once implemented, the internal help system), and Quit (which shuts down the client).
The tabs at the bottom of the Messages pane allow selection of a communication mode.

note.para: At present, only text chat works. Grayed out elements in the &chat_client; interface are not yet implemented.

section.para: Despite appearances, &chat_client;'s emphasis on anonymity means that familiar terms take on new meanings, particularly the idea of a "contact."

listitem.para: Contact names are arbitrary. Contacts in one conversation are unconnected with contacts in other conversations. Each chat participant can choose a unique name for each conversation.
&chat_client; and &program_name; operate with no information about the real-world identities behind contacts. There are no e-mail addresses, telephone numbers, postal addresses, or anything similar.

Without phone numbers or email as anchors for identity, &chat_client; users require a real-world encounter to verify who they are and to share cryptographic secrets. This kind of contact bootstrapping occurs out-of-band (OOB), that is, without reliance on the primary communication channel, which is &chat_client;. The concept is similar to the practice of PGP email users who hold in-person key-signing parties to build a web of trust.

section.para: The first thing that a new user of &chat_client; must do is create a conversation. This must happen before you can invite contacts or accept invitations.

step.para: Open &chat_client;. Until a conversation has been created, the Messages pane prompts you to create one.
In the toolbar, click the New conversation button.

In the New conversation window, type a name in the Choose conversation name field. This name is how you identify the conversation in your own &chat_client; client. It may differ from what your contact calls their corresponding conversation. Click OK when finished.
In the following screen capture, the New conversation field is being filled out.

caption.para: Figure 2. In this example, a user creates a first conversation called My first conversation.

step.para: Type a name for yourself in the field labeled Choose (your) name displayed to the other user(s). Your contacts will see this name when they accept your invitation.
The following screen capture shows a name that was typed in by the user.

caption.para: Figure 3. The user types in "Max" as his name in the context of this conversation.

step.para: Click OK when finished.
Now, in the Conversations and contacts pane, the name of your new conversation is displayed along with your display name. In the Messages pane, &chat_client; prints a greeting message.
The final result resembles the following:

caption.para: Figure 4. In the Conversations and contacts pane, you can select a conversation. The selected conversation will be displayed in the Messages pane. You can use the Type to filter contacts text box to find a specific contact name and the conversations that contain it.

section.para: You can create any number of conversations, each one separated completely from other conversations.

Once you have a created a conversation, you can begin adding contacts to it. As a user of &chat_client;, you have no fixed user name or password; instead, you assign a name of your choosing for each conversation and potentially for each contact.

A user setting up a contact generates an authentication token called a voucher. The voucher is a Base64-encoded string with the following contents:
a display name
a mixnet storage address that doubles as read permission

A user who makes a request for a new contact delivers the voucher out-of-band to one or more recipients, who enter the invitation string into &chat_client; and, by accepting it, send their own addresses and signed read permissions to the first user, who publishes the shared read permissions for all group members to see. When the process is complete, the new contact names display in the list of contacts for each participant in the conversation.

caption.para: Figure 5. The diagram illustrates two important aspects of &program_name; and &chat_client; security. First, the initial authentication of a contact is done in a face-to-face meeting rather than electronically. Second, all messaging consists of queries to the mixnet, which operates somewhat as a dead-drop. Max and Moritz post materials there, and authorize each other to read those materials, but there is no direct contact between them after the initial real-world meeting.

important.para: We recommend writing the invitation string on a piece paper, and presenting this physically to the person or persons you are inviting. The paper bearing the string should be guarded carefully and destroyed after use.

warning.para: It is possible to simply send your invitation through an alternative electronic channel. However, doing this permanently degrades the &program_name; anonymity protections to the level of anonymity offered by the channel that you used.

step.para: Open &chat_client; as described above.
With the desired conversation selected, click Invite a contact in the Messages pane.
In the Invite contact window, type your desired display name in the field labeled Choose (your) name displayed to the other user, then click OK.
The following screen capture shows the Invite contact window with "Max" specified as the issuer.

caption.para: Figure 6. The invitation string has "Max" embedded as its creator, which is helpful to the recipient in the next steps.

step.para:
A pop-up window displays the Base64 string that was created. Save this string long enough to copy it to paper or save electronically.
Figure 7. The voucher's Base64 string is highlighted in the illustration. Record it before closing the window.
Complete the invitation process by providing the invitation string out-of-band to your intended contact.

para.emphasis: To accept an invitation that you have received

step.para: Open &chat_client;. (In the following example, our perspective shifts to Moritz, who is the user receiving Max's invitation.)
In the toolbar, click Accept invitation.
In the Accept invitation window, type or paste the invitation string into the field labeled Enter an invitation you received. Your client should resemble the following:

caption.para: Figure 8. Moritz has entered the invitation string into the Accept invitation window.

step.para: To approve the display name of the new contact, click Yes. To cancel the acceptance process, click No.

caption.para: Figure 9. Moritz can either accept or reject Max's display name. Rejecting it cancels the acceptance.

step.para: Moritz must start the same procedure in reverse. In his selected conversation, he clicks Invite contact, generates a Base64 string, and conveys it to Max. Max clicks Accept invitation, types the Base64 string into his client, and clicks OK twice.

section.para: As shown below, Max and Moritz now appear in each other's contact lists, and they can begin exchanging messages. The procedures described here can be generalized to groups of any size.

note.para: When you look at the perspectives of Max and Moritz side-by-side, as in Figure 10 below, something strange pops out: Their (shared?) conversation has two different names. This provides a glimpse into the anonymity architecture behind &chat_client;, and is explained in the FAQ: xxxxxxx

caption.para: Figure 10. Max and Moritz are shown with their respective conversations and contact lists.

section.title: Exchanging messages in a conversation
section.para: &chat_client; resembles other chat programs in its procedure for exchanging messages. This section provides an example of a conversation between two participants.

procedure.title: To exchange messages between two contacts
procedure.para: This procedure picks up where the previous section, , left off. The examples show both sides of the Max/Moritz conversation.

step.para: Max composes a message to Moritz by typing it in the Single-line message box at the bottom of the Messages pane, as shown in the following screen capture.

caption.para: Figure 11. Max can see what conversation he is in by looking at the highlighted conversation name in Conversations and contacts pane, and at the heading in the Messages pane.

step.para: When Max is done typing the message, he presses Enter to send it.

caption.para: Figure 12. Max's sent message is visible in his Messages pane. The in-flight arrow next to his name indicates that Moritz has not yet received the message, as is apparent in his &chat_client; window.

step.para: In the following screen capture, Moritz has received Max's message.

caption.para: Figure 13. Moritz's &chat_client; window now displays Max's message, and the in-flight arrow has disappeared from Max's window.

step.para: In the next screen capture, Moritz types and sends a reply to Max.

caption.para: Figure 14. With Moritz's message sent, his Messages pane shows the in-flight arrow pending delivery.

step.para: In this last screen capture, Max has received Moritz's reply and they continued to converse.

caption.para: Figure 15. Success! Several messages have been exchanged and the absence of in-flight arrows indicates that no messages are pending at the moment.
